Learning Objectives
List the contributions of the scapula in scapulohumeral rhythm.
Identify the anatomic components critical to proper scapular function.
Describe motions and muscle activations that create the scapular mechanics (i.e., the rotations
and translations of the scapula).
Describe the role of the scapula in normal shoulder function and in individuals with shoulder
pain and/or various shoulder pathology.
Define scapular dyskinesis.
Describe the clinical examination algorithm used to determine the presence or absence of
scapular dyskinesis, the role of the scapula with regard to the clinical symptoms, and the
causative factors underlying the dyskinesis.
Explain specific clinical maneuvers to identify scapular dysfunction and its causative factors.
Employ kinetic chain exercises to manage scapular dysfunction.

Anatomy
Overview
Ideal scapular function reflects the complex anatomy of the scapula and, therefore, is
foundational for all shoulder function.
The scapula plays multiple roles. Anatomically, it is the “G” of the glenohumeral joint and the
“A” of the acromioclavicular joint. Physiologically, it is the “S” of scapulohumeral rhythm (SHR),
the coupled and coordinated movement between the scapula and arm that allows the arm to
be placed in the optimal position and motion to accomplish tasks. Biomechanically, it provides
a stable base for muscle activation, a moving platform to maintain ball-and-socket kinematics,
and an efficient link between the core, which develops force, and the arm, which delivers the
force. Critical to these roles is normal scapular motion.
Bony connections are limited, allowing large ranges of motion.
Numerous muscular attachments produce a wide range of scapular and humeral movement,
and various sets of rotations and translations are available to achieve those movements.
Osteology
The bony anatomy reflects the need for a balance of stability and mobility.
The scapular body is a thin sheet of bone that serves as a site of muscle attachment.
The acromion provides a bony arch over the glenohumeral joint and rotator cuff, creating a
subacromial space.
The glenoid serves as the socket for the ball-and-socket kinematics of the glenohumeral joint.
The clavicle is the only bony connection to the axial skeleton.

Osteology
The scapula typically spans the second to seventh ribs and has three borders: medial,
lateral, and inferior. Approximately 6% of scapulae have a hook-shaped prominence
known as a Luschka tubercle at the superomedial angle. The dorsal surface is traversed

by the scapular spine, which divides two concavities: the supraspinatus and
infraspinatus fossae. The spine contains two important notches. The suprascapular
notch is located at the lateral portion of the superior scapular border near the base of
the coracoid process. The transverse scapular ligament extends across the notch, with
the suprascapular artery lying above the ligament and the suprascapular nerve running
below the ligament. The spinoglenoid notch lies below the lateral border of the scapular
spine with the suprascapular artery and nerve passing through it. Variability of the
spinoglenoid ligament (inferior transverse scapular ligament) exists.
It has been described as pear-shaped, and its rather shallow depth allows a great
amount of glenohumeral joint mobility while creating the possibility of excessive
glenohumeral joint instability.
Its articulation with the sternum through the sternoclavicular joint allows for a wide
range of elevation/depression motion, anterior/posterior motion, and rotation along its
long axis. Its curved, crank handle–shaped anatomy enables a wide range of scapular
motions. Its stable articulation with the scapula through the acromion (acromioclavicular
joint) facilitates optimal three-dimensional screw axis motion of the two bones.
Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply is primarily through a network of periosteal vessels, which take origin from
muscular insertions.
Nerves
The spinal accessory nerve runs in the posterior triangle of the neck between the posterior
border of the sternocleidomastoid and the anterior border of the upper trapezius. It then
travels with the superficial branch of the transverse cervical artery along the central aspect of
the levator scapulae and deep to the trapezius.
The dorsal scapular nerve and artery lie deep to the levator scapulae and the rhomboid minor
and major and course approximately 2 to 3 cm medial to the vertebral border of the scapula.
The long thoracic nerve courses along the anterior margin of the serratus anterior.

The suprascapular nerve (C5/6) originates from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus and
courses toward the suprascapular notch with the suprascapular artery.
Joints and Ligaments
Glenohumeral joint
Acromioclavicular joint
The coracoacromial ligament limits the cantilever effect between the acromion and coracoid.
Coracoclavicular ligaments
Sternoclavicular joint

Joints and Ligaments
It is the articulation between the glenoid fossa of the scapula and the head of the
humerus. Its anatomy and physiology are responsible for the large amount of mobility
while maintaining some inherent stability. The glenohumeral ligaments are primarily
responsible for providing stability at the end ranges of glenohumeral motion. Bony
alignment, the glenoid labrum, and coordinated muscle activations are primarily
responsible for providing glenohumeral stability in the midranges of glenohumeral
motion.
It is the articulation between the acromion and the clavicle. Its relatively rigid anatomy
creates an inherently stable linkage between the two bones, allowing for coupled
motion. The acromioclavicular ligament complex has three components: anterior,
posterior, and superior. They provide anterior and posterior stabilization between the
clavicle and acromion, lateral stability as a tension band, and rotational stability of the
clavicle on the scapula and the scapula on the clavicle.
The coracoclavicular ligament complex has two components: the conoid and the
trapezoid. It provides suspension to the scapula under the clavicle and acts as a force
transducer between the two bones, allowing force or motion to be transmitted between
the two bones. The conoid ligament has a vertical orientation and attachment that
provides suspensory function and tightens with scapular rotation, creating a stable

claviscapular linkage. The trapezoid ligament has a diagonal orientation and attachment
that provides lateral stability.
It is the articulation between the clavicle and the axial skeleton. The sternoclavicular
ligaments stabilize the proximal clavicle to optimize clavicle stability and mobility for
three-dimensional scapular motions.
Musculature
Movement of the scapula in arm function is the result of coordinated activation of many of the
17 muscles that attach to the scapula.
The muscles responsible for the largest amount of scapular movement are present in three
layers: superficial, intermediate, and deep.

Musculature
The superficial layer consists of the trapezius and the latissimus dorsi. The trapezius
inserts on the scapular spine, acromion, and clavicle and acts as the primary provider for
scapular stabilization and as an important provider of scapular motion. The upper
trapezius originates from the cervical spine and attaches on the lateral clavicle. The
middle trapezius originates from the cervical, upper thoracic spine and attaches to the
lateral acromion. The lower trapezius has a broad origin from the thoracic spine and
attaches to the scapular spine. The latissimus dorsi may have occasional attachments to
the inferior angle of the scapula.
The intermediate layer consists of the levator scapulae and the rhomboids. The levator
scapulae originates from the cervical spine and inserts on the superomedial angle of the
scapula. The rhomboid major originates from the thoracic spine and inserts on the
medial border of the scapula from the level of the scapular spine and below. The
rhomboid minor originates from the cervical spine and inserts on the medial border of
the scapula above the rhomboid major.

The deep layer consists of the serratus anterior and superior and the pectoralis minor.
The serratus originates from the upper ribs eight and nine and inserts on the entire
medial border of the scapula. The pectoralis minor originates from the coracoid process
and inserts on ribs four through six.
Other Structures
Two anatomic (major) and four adventitial (minor) bursae at the scapulothoracic articulation
have been described. The two anatomic (major) bursae include the infraserratus
(scapulothoracic) bursa and the supraserratus (subscapularis) bursa.
Mechanics
Scapular motion optimizes the balance between scapular stability, serving as a base for
glenohumeral motion and scapular mobility in coordination with arm motion.1
Scapular motion is coupled with clavicular and humeral motion to create SHR.2 Scapular
motion can be divided into four phases.
The scapula and clavicle are mechanically linked to create the claviscapular segment in two of
the phases.
Coordinated muscle activations produce scapular and claviscapular motions.3,4
Scapular kinematics: normal patterns of individual motions of the scapula with arm motion.

Mechanics
Scapular stability provides a stable base for optimal activation of the scapular-based
muscles, a stable fulcrum for arm function as a first-class and third-class lever, and
stability against the loads and momentum of arm motion. Scapular mobility provides a
dynamic socket for optimal glenohumeral joint ball-and-socket kinematics, creating
maximal concavity/compression and dynamic glenohumeral stability throughout the
entire arm motion; results in positioning the arm and hand in three-dimensional space
for function; and moves the acromion for optimal arm elevation.

SHR represents coupled motions between the scapula and the arm that have been
shown to be the key actions to create optimal shoulder and arm function. Efficient SHR
underlies efficient arm function, and alterations in SHR affect effective arm function and
increase injury risk. The amount of coupled motion can be described as a ratio between
individual scapular and humeral motions during arm movement in elevation. The mean
ratio between scapular rotation and humeral rotation over entire arm motion up to
maximal elevation is 1:2. The ratio varies from 1:1 to 1:4 depending on the phases of
scapular and arm motion.
Three sets of rotations exist: upward/downward rotation around a horizontal
anteroposterior axis, anterior/posterior tilt around a horizontal mediolateral axis, and
internal/external rotation around a vertical axis (Video 1). Three sets of translations
occur in the presence of an intact clavicle/acromioclavicular joint strut:
elevation/depression (Video 2), lateral translation (Video 3), and medial translation
(Video 4). The terms protraction and retraction describe terminal translation positions
after lateral and medial translation, respectively.

Functional scapular motions are a composite of the sets of rotations and can be divided
into four phases. The result is that the scapula performs two roles to facilitate task-
specific arm activities in SHR. The first role is to position the glenoid and the
glenohumeral joint in the correct three-dimensional position to optimize arm position.
The second role is to move in coordination with the humerus through all ranges of
motion to accomplish the specific task.
Phase 1 involves setting the scapula and occurs during 0° to 30° of arm elevation. This
creates the initial placement to optimize further and later arm motions. The primary
muscle activation for motion is the serratus anterior. The SHR ratio is 1:4.
Phase 2 involves scapular rotation and occurs during 30° to 100° of arm elevation. This
results in mainly upward rotation in three-dimensional task-specific patterns. The
scapula rotates as a claviscapular unit: the two bones are linked and stabilized by
development of tension in the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments and the
acromioclavicular joint. The primary muscle activation for mobilization is the serratus
anterior, and the primary muscle activation for control and stabilization is the trapezius.

The sternoclavicular joint is the pivot point for this rotation, creating an instant center of
rotation at the medial scapular spine. The SHR ratio is 1:1.
Phase 3 involves scapular rotation at or above 100° of arm elevation. Motion of the
claviscapular segment results in mainly posterior rotation along the long axis of the
clavicle. The muscle activations to produce this rotation are the serratus anterior and the
trapezius, producing scapular posterior tilt and external rotation. The force transducers
to produce clavicular rotation are the coracoclavicular and acromioclavicular ligaments.
The instant center of rotation moves along the clavicle to the acromioclavicular joint.
Little SHR rotation occurs. This phase mainly positions the scapula to act as a base for
glenohumeral function.
Phase 4 is characterized by controlled dynamic scapular stability at or above 100°. The
exact position depends on the required tasks and demands for function. The scapula
performs as a stable base for glenohumeral function, optimizing concavity/compression
and muscle activation. At this level, the most effective single scapular position and
motion for arm function is stabilized retraction, consisting of external rotation, posterior
tilt, and upward rotation. For dynamic overhead activities, controlled protraction also is
required to respond to the eccentric activities experienced during throwing.
For upward rotation, the primary activation is the serratus anterior (superior fibers) with
assistance from the middle trapezius (Figure 1). Secondarily, the lower trapezius acts as
a checkrein for limiting excessive elevation, and the upper trapezius acts to elevate the
distal clavicle and acromion to avoid humeral contact. As the arm is elevated into
forward flexion, the upper portion of the serratus anterior contracts, pulling the medial
border of the scapula anteriorly around the ellipsoid thorax. Although the exact point of
humeral elevation is unknown, the middle trapezius begins to assist the serratus
anterior by pulling the upper portion of the scapula medial toward the vertebral column,
increasing upward rotation. During these muscle contractions, the lower trapezius helps
prevent the scapula from elevating excessively during upward rotation while the upper
trapezius acts to elevate the distal clavicle and acromion to avoid contact between the
acromion and the humeral head.

For downward rotation, the primary activation is the rhomboids and the lower trapezius.
As the arm is lowered from an elevated position, the attachment of the rhomboids to the
medial scapular border and the attachment of the lower trapezius to the spine of the

For posterior tilt, the primary activation is coupled activity of the lower trapezius and the

occurs because of the attachment of the serratus anterior to the inferior angle of the
scapula. Assistance is provided by the lower trapezius, which attaches to the deltoid
tubercle on the scapular spine.

Figure 2 Image of a scapula shows how posterior tilt occurs via activation of the inferior

For anterior tilt, the primary activation is the pectoralis minor and secondarily the
pectoralis major. As the arm is lowered from an elevated position, the pectoralis minor
pulls the scapula anteriorly via its attachment to the coracoid process. Anterior tilt also
may occur passively because of an imbalance between the posterior scapular muscles
and the anterior muscles along with the weight of the arm. The anterior muscles are
larger and often are more powerful compared with the posterior muscles, creating a
tendency for the arm to migrate forward.
For external rotation, the primary activation is the rhomboids and the superior fibers of
the serratus anterior (Figure 3). At terminal arm elevation, the rhomboids and the
serratus anterior oppose each other, creating external rotation of the scapula. Each
muscle has a diagonal orientation but in opposing directions. As each muscle contracts,
the medial border and body of the scapula rotates externally around a vertical axis
running through the body of the scapula.

For internal rotation, the primary activation is the pectoralis minor and secondarily the
pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, and deltoid. As the arm is lowered from an elevated
position, the pectoralis minor helps the scapula return from the externally rotated
position achieved at terminal elevation by pulling the scapula internally around the
vertical axis. Similar to the mechanism described for anterior tilting, internal rotation
also may occur passively because of an imbalance between the posterior scapular
muscles and the anterior muscles along with the weight of the arm.
For elevation, the primary activation is the upper trapezius, rhomboids, and levator
scapulae (Figure 4). The shoulder shrug occurs because of contraction of the upper
trapezius, rhomboids, and levator scapulae muscles. Elevation occurs as these muscles
contract because of the diagonal attachments at the lateral clavicle (upper trapezius), the
medial border of the scapula (rhomboids), and the superior angle of the scapula (levator
scapulae).

An example of functional coupled motions is the overhead throwing motion. The
scapular kinematics demonstrate that the scapula upwardly rotates, tilts posteriorly, and
externally rotates as the humerus is brought into maximal abduction.3 From this point,
as the humerus externally rotates during acceleration, the scapula further upwardly
rotates, externally rotates, and posteriorly tilts, creating maximal scapular retraction at
the late cocking phase.4 During stride foot contact, the scapula retracts, upwardly
rotates, and anteriorly tilts.5,6 Progression to ball release results in anterior tilting and
internal rotation. After ball release, the humerus continues to internally rotate with
maximal internal rotation, downward rotation, and anterior tilting of the scapula.3 This
position dissipates the remaining force generated during ball acceleration and
represents the opposite extreme of scapular motion during humeral maximal external
rotation.5,6

Driving these scapular kinematics, the muscle activations demonstrate that as a pitcher
strides and the humerus is brought into abduction and external rotation, the scapula
begins to retract, consistent with findings of concentric activation of the serratus
anterior and the upper and middle trapezius. With the transition from early cocking to
late cocking, increased middle trapezius firing and less upper trapezius activation occur,
allowing the abducted humerus to externally rotate without impingement. The levator
scapulae and the serratus anterior eccentrically and isometrically fire to stabilize the
scapula as the shoulder reaches maximum external rotation before firing concentrically
to protract the scapula and assist the arm with acceleration. During acceleration, all the
tested scapula-stabilizing muscles have high activity, and the three segments of the
trapezius fire equally to support the position changes of the humeral head. As the arm
decelerates, the lower trapezius has the greatest function, with moderate activity of the
upper trapezius, serratus anterior, and rhomboids. These actions control scapula
protraction and aid in dissipating forces as the humerus internally rotates. The muscles
relax during follow-through because all muscle activity decreases, with the serratus
anterior having the greatest stabilizing activation during this phase.7,8
Scapular Function and Dysfunction (Scapular Dyskinesis)
The roles of the scapula in optimizing and facilitating shoulder and arm function and in
contributing to shoulder and arm dysfunction
Scapular dyskinesis (dys: alteration of; kinesis: motion)
Causative factors that have been associated with scapular dyskinesis

Scapular Function and Dysfunction (Scapular Dyskinesis)
The scapula plays several roles as it functions to maximize efficient SHR, including acting
as a transfer link for force from its development in the hip/core to its use at the hand,9
being a stable base for optimal scapular-based muscle activation,10 maintaining optimal
position to produce a congruent socket for dynamic ball-and-socket
concavity/compression and glenohumeral stability, and providing acromial motion to
allow for maximum arm motion and elevation.11-14

Scapular dyskinesis results from alterations in the normal scapular roles, which create
dysfunctions that limit efficient SHR; represent alterations in functional roles; and create
an impairment of scapular positioning, optimal force transfer, muscle activations,
scapular motion with arm motion, and dynamic stability. They can be demonstrated in
67% to 100% of patients with shoulder injuries.15 They may represent a cause or an
effect of the shoulder injury.
Scapular dyskinesis is defined as an observable, abnormal, asymmetric scapular position
at rest characterized by medial border or inferior medial border prominence (Figure 8;
Video 5); abnormal anterior scapular tilt and protraction; abnormal upward shrug; or a
SICK (Scapular malpositioning, Inferior medial border prominence, Coracoid pain and
malpositioning, and dyskinesis of scapular movement) scapula (characterized by inferior
and lateral tilting; observable abnormal asymmetric scapular motion with arm motion
consisting of medial border or inferior angle prominence, which may increase with more
arm motion; scapular elevation or shrugging early in arm elevation; or rapid downward
rotation during arm lowering).16 The final result of the altered position or motion is
scapular protraction at rest or on arm motion. Occasionally, dyskinesis may be a
asymptomatic finding, and it may be clinically important in the presence of other
anatomic, physiologic, and/or mechanical factors.17 Regardless whether associated with
symptoms, protraction is an unfavorable position for almost all shoulder functions and
may increase the risk of subsequent injury. If it is demonstrated on physical examination
in a symptomatic patient or a patient who anticipates high loads during overhead
activities, one of the goals of treatment or conditioning should be regaining static and
dynamic retraction capability.

Physical Examination
Overview
A clinically useful and reliable physical examination can identify dyskinesis and serve as a basis
for mangaement.16,19,20
The goals of the physical examination of the scapula are to establish the presence or absence
of altered scapular position at rest; identify the presence of scapular dyskinesis; evaluate joint,
muscle, and bone and nerve causative factors; and use dynamic corrective maneuvers to
assess the effect of correcting dyskinesis on patient symptoms.16

instructed to extend the trunk and push the hand maximally against an examiner’s
resistance in the direction of shoulder extension and to retract and depress the scapula.

providing the examiner with a visual depiction of lower trapezius muscle contraction.

The kinetic chain screening assessment26 uses the one-leg stability series, which
assesses a patient’s capability of controlling the trunk and body over the planted leg.
This assessment includes two components. The first component is the single-leg
standing balance test, which evaluates dynamic control of position (Video 8). The patient
is asked to place the hands over the chest and stand on one leg with no other verbal cue.
Deviations, such as a Trendelenburg posture or internally or externally rotating the
weight-bearing limb, indicate inability to control the posture and correlates with
proximal core weakness, especially in the gluteus medius.27 The second component is
the single-leg squat test, which evaluates dynamic control of motion (Video 9). Assuming
the same starting point as the standing balance test, the patient is asked to perform
repetitive partial half squats going down and returning to the standing position with no
other verbal cues. Possible deviations indicate poor core control. A Trendelenburg
posture may not be noted on standing balance but may be brought out with a single-leg
squat. The patient also may use his or her arms for balance or may go into an
exaggerated flexed or rotated posture—corkscrewing— to put the gluteal or short
rotator muscles on greater tension to compensate for muscular weakness.28 A valgus
knee position during the descent phase of the squat likely indicates weakness of
dynamic stabilization from the pelvis to the knee.

To obtain accurate glenohumeral internal rotation measurements,30 the patient should

The scapular muscle strength assessment must be performed to evaluate the individual
muscles and their strength because the scapula is a muscle-dominant bone. The
serratus anterior, innervated by the long thoracic nerve, has a considerable contribution

correct the problem with appropriate cueing and also may perform normally on a

Because glenohumeral internal derangement may be associated with scapular
dyskinesis, as a cause or as an effect, a comprehensive clinical examination of the
glenohumeral joint via standard examination techniques should be performed, with
emphasis on evaluation of labral injury and glenohumeral instability.
Causative factors for dyskinesis may be grouped into soft-tissue, bone/joint, or
neurologic factors. Soft-tissue factors include hip/core weakness with altered facilitation
of muscle activation;49,50 altered periscapular and shoulder muscle activation,
coordination, or balance because of pain-derived muscle inhibition or fatigue;51 muscle
stiffness and tightness;29,52 loss of voluntary control of muscle activation;53,54 or
posttraumatic periscapular muscle injury.55,56 Bone/joint causes include clavicle
shortening, angulation, or malrotation; acromioclavicular/sternoclavicular joint arthritis
or instability; or glenohumeral joint internal derangement. Neurologic causes include

Specific Injuries Associated With Scapular Dyskinesis
Soft-Tissue–Related Scapular Dyskinesis
Dyskinesis will be observed secondary to alterations in muscle strength, balance, activation,
inhibition, or posture locally and in the kinetic chain.57
It can be managed primarily via nonsurgical treatment options, emphasizing restoration of the
deficits found on clinical examination.
Effective treatment protocols require a comprehensive evaluation for local and distant
causative factors, ruling out surgically related diagnoses.

Internal rotation deficits are common in overhead athletes, with the throwing arm
having approximately 10° less of internal rotation than the nonthrowing arm,58-60 with
side-to-side differences as much as 45° observed in symptomatic athletes. This rotation
loss has been proposed to result from bony, capsular, and/or muscular changes over
time.31,61-66
Muscle activation imbalance may create dyskinesis. The most common alteration is loss
of coordination of the upper trapezius/lower trapezius force couple, in which the lower
trapezius activates later and with less amplitude.49 Loss of coordinated muscle
activation, producing scapular dyskinesis, also is observed because of inhibition from
glenohumeral joint injury. External impingement, labral injury, biceps pathology, rotator
cuff disease, glenohumeral instability, and adhesive capsulitis have been associated with
alterations in lower trapezius, upper trapezius, and serratus anterior activation that
result in scapular protraction and dyskinesis.10,19 The dyskinesis may increase the
dysfunction from the injury and may delay functional recovery if not included in the
comprehensive rehabilitation plan.

Neurologically Based Scapular Winging With Dyskinesis
Long thoracic nerve injury may be very disruptive to SHR and arm function. It creates
loss of the serratus anterior muscle function to control the inferior medial tip, which
causes the inferior angle to become notably prominent on static and dynamic
examination. The main clinical dysfunction on examination is inability to elevate the arm
above 90° because of loss of scapular control. The diagnosis can be confirmed on
electromyography (EMG) approximately 6 weeks after initial trauma. The clinical
presentation involves pain because of fatigability secondary to the other periscapular
muscles compensating. More severe pain may be indicative of brachial plexus neuritis
(Parsonage-Turner syndrome). On physical examination, the scapula is elevated
superiorly (anterior tilt), with a prominent medial border and medial rotation of the
inferior pole (Video 12). Shoulder elevation above 110° cannot be accomplished because
of loss of scapular control. This may lead to the development of external (subacromial)
impingement because of poor acromial elevation. This winging is most pronounced with
forward elevation but also may be exacerbated with resisted forward elevation
(observed while attempting wall push-ups). Resolution/improvement may be observed

chest wall) or the SRT. The etiology usually is damage (blunt trauma or stretching in

The scapula is a large flat bone that forms from a collection of mesenchymal cells.69 It
shows signs of ossification by the fifth week of embryologic development.69 The scapula
follows a predictable course in descending from the paracervical region to the thorax.
Failure of this process leads to Sprengel deformity (ie, high-riding scapula) or
prominence of the superomedial border.70 This congenital anomaly of scapular
development results in the scapula remaining small and undescended secondary to an
interruption of the embryonic subclavian blood supply. This leads to scapular hypoplasia
and winging with limited scapulothoracic motion. Patients typically have deficiencies in
forward elevation and abduction. Patients may require surgical treatment for severe
functional deformities, with surgical treatment ideally being performed between ages 3
to 8 years (patients >8 years have an increased risk of nerve injury). Advanced imaging
studies should be obtained to assess for an omovertebral bar connecting the
superomedial border of the scapulae to one of the lower cervical vertebrae.

motions of posterior tilt and external rotation are decreased as the arm elevates.
Consequently, the normal movement of the instant center of rotation of the scapula
from the superomedial border to the acromioclavicular joint is disrupted, causing the
scapula to rotate around the medial border, creating excessive pressure and leading to
symptoms.73
Patients generally report periscapular pain during overhead activities. The throwing
motion, with its large scapular excursion, is particularly affected. Patients often notice an
audible grinding or snapping, amplified by the thoracic cavity, which may be precipitated
by active range of motion or simply by shrugging. The superomedial border is most
common location of pain. Because of the abnormal mechanics, the cause of crepitus is
believed to be the chronically inflamed bursa. In few patients, an anatomic abnormality,
such as osteochondromas or a malunited rib fracture, disrupts the scapulothoracic
articulation and creates a predisposition to snapping scapula.

treatment directed at the individual patient’s etiologic factors. The cornerstone usually is
physical therapy focused on proper postural and periscapular mechanics. The lower
trapezius and the serratus anterior are strengthened via isometric and dynamic
endurance training. The contracted anterior muscles should be mobilized via massage
and stretching. Activity modifications and physical therapy modalities may be included.
Scapular bracing may be useful for some patients. Bursal inflammation can be managed
via precise injections placed via appropriate technique and caution.

One of the salient features of multidirectional instability is that symptoms and instability

Rehabilitation
Optimal rehabilitation of scapular dyskinesis requires management of all the causative
factors that create the dyskinesis and restoration of the balance of muscle forces that
allow for scapular position and motion. Inflexibility factors include shoulder rotation
tightness (glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and total range of motion deficit);81
pectoralis minor inflexibility;29 and muscular factors, including lower trapezius and
serratus anterior weakness, upper trapezius hyperactivity, and kinetic chain factors
including hip/leg weakness and core weakness.9 The bone and joint internal
derangement factors may require surgical management before rehabilitation is
maximally effective.
Scapular-based programs should differ from traditional shoulder strengthening
programs in key areas. Although seminal studies identified maneuvers that can activate
high amounts of electrical activity in the shoulder and scapular muscles, the
foundational work was performed on asymptomatic individuals.82-86 Patients with a
painful and/or injured shoulder may not tolerate such high-demand maneuvers. The
identified maneuvers often were performed in an isolated manner with the body in a
vertical or horizontal stationary position. Considering the scapula as a link in the kinetic
chain, these isolated maneuvers may not reestablish scapular mobility and control in the
necessary motor patterns that require integrated use of most of the kinetic chain
segments. Failure to incorporate the kinetic chain throughout the rehabilitation process,
from the earlier phases of management through the later phases, may lead to less than
optimal rehabilitation outcomes. Therefore, to fully use the kinetic chain (legs, pelvis,
and trunk), positioning patients in standing positions is preferred. In some patients, the
scapula and shoulder may be overtly dysfunctional. In these patients, minimizing the
degrees of freedom via the elimination of gravity-dependent positions may be
necessary; therefore, sitting positions may be used.25,87 Restoration of the scapular
muscle force couples requires core strength and facilitation via kinetic chain
activation.87,88 This establishes the proximal stability to prevent postural perturbation
and force generation and maximizes activation sequencing for the scapular retraction

After successful reattachment of the muscles (Figure 20), an external rotation sling is
used for 4 weeks postoperatively. Internal rotation and abduction are not allowed for 3
weeks postoperatively, and active forward flexion is not allowed for 6 weeks
postoperatively. During the first 3 weeks postoperatively, the patient permitted to
perform active scapular retraction and depression. All patients are referred to formal
physical therapy after the fourth postoperative week and are provided with a
standardized closed kinetic chain protocol designed to minimize shear forces at the
glenohumeral joint and increase proprioceptive feedback through the shoulder and
scapula. Additional rehabilitation measures, such as the use of modalities, manual
therapy (except for thoracic mobilizations, which are prohibited by the protocol), and
other exercises for lower body rehabilitation, are permitted. Active forward flexion and
abduction up to 90° of elevation should be permitted at 6 weeks postoperatively,
